answers.implementation_then_now: 2023: the TIP Report 2022 (covering 2021) says that all identified adult trafficking victims were foreigners and asks Chile to screen vulnerable migrants. That report is about trafficking victims, not about wage equality as such. 2026: ENCLA 2023, as reported in the press in 2025, finds a significant pay gap between migrants and Chileans, with informality, underemployment and low pay; Haitians are concentrated in fixed-term and per-job contracts. The 2025 TIP Report (covering 2024) records rising numbers of foreign labour-trafficking victims. Neither period shows a shift: the gaps are documented on both dates, and nothing in the window points to a change. The starting rating is kept for both dates.

practice_sources.title: Sueldos de migrantes en Chile: 66% gana $800 mil bruto (ENCLA 2023), El Desconcierto

answers.sourcing_note: I read Ley 21.325 on LeyChile in its original version (12 February 2022), its intermediate version of 1 April 2025 (in force on 1 January 2026) and its current version; arts. 13 and 14 are identical in all three. For art. 2 of the Labour Code I read the current consolidated text with its amendment notes, plus the text of Ley 21.643. I could not open Ley 21.675 (PDF unreadable) or the Fundación SOL study.
answers.starting_answer_concern: 'Effectively Always' looks too high. ENCLA 2023 and studies based on CASEN data document a significant migrant–Chilean pay gap, part of it unexplained for Venezuelans, and high informality. 'Usually' or 'Sometimes; Usually' would fit the MRD's usual practice better. The citation's 'Labour Code article 1' should be article 2, inciso cuarto, which lists 'nacionalidad' as a prohibited ground. Ley 21.325 art. 14 carries the equal-labour-rights rule: 'Los extranjeros gozarán de los mismos derechos en materia laboral que los chilenos'.
answers.notes: Relied on statutes only, not court rulings. Four laws amended Ley 21.325 in the window (21.590, 21.589, 21.610 and 21.655). A comparison of the versions shows they did not touch arts. 13 or 14. Constitution art. 19 N°16 ('libre elección del trabajo con una justa retribución') carries no amendment note after 2005.

answers.answer_2023: Migrant workers have completely free choice of employment
answers.answer_2026: Migrant workers have completely free choice of employment
answers.change_2023_2026: There have been right protections both in 2023 and 2026 and neither the right protection nor the implementation level of these protections has changed

provisions.instrument: Decreto 177 (2022), Ministerio del Interior y Seguridad Pública, establece las subcategorías migratorias de residencia temporal

answers.implementation_then_now: No source I found documents the immigration authority blocking a change of employer, on either date. Decreto 177 art. 19 provides that a holder of the work-based temporary permit may change employer without informing SERMIG. The labour-trafficking findings in the 2022 and 2025 TIP reports concern exploitation, not legal tying to an employer. I found no practice evidence specific to employer changes in either period, so the starting rating is carried forward unchanged.
answers.sourcing_note: In Ley 21.325, art. 73 ('Los residentes temporales podrán desarrollar actividades remuneradas') reads the same in the 2022, 2025 and current versions, and I read art. 70 in the current version. LeyChile lists Decreto 177 as 'Versión: Única - 14-MAY-2022', so it was never amended. The practice evidence is indirect.
answers.starting_answer_concern: Decreto 177 art. 19 does support free change of employer: 'podrá cambiar de empleador sin necesidad de informarlo al Servicio Nacional de Migraciones'. Two limits weigh against 'completely free'. First, the work permit is first granted on the strength of a specific contract (art. 17), and the seasonal permit is capped at 6 months per year. Second, Labour Code art. 19, unchanged, requires that at least 85% of the workers of any employer with more than 25 employees be Chilean. A reviewer could reasonably judge the 'completely free' answer generous, and the 'Effectively Always' rating rests on no documented practice.
answers.notes: No ruling in the window was found. Labour Code art. 19 (85% national-workers quota) carries no amendment note in the window.

answers.change_2023_2026: There have been no right protections neither in 2023 nor in 2026

provisions.instrument: Ley 21.325 de Migración y Extranjería (not cited by the starting answer; checked)

answers.implementation_then_now: Because the starting answer is 'No', implementation is 'Does Not Apply' on both dates. I found no practice evidence on dependants' work in either period. The relevant law did not change between 2023 and 2026.
answers.sourcing_note: Art. 74 of Ley 21.325 reads the same in the original (2022), 1 April 2025 and current versions. Decreto 177 has a single version (14 May 2022).
answers.starting_answer_concern: The starting 'No' looks wrong. Ley 21.325 art. 74, in force unchanged since 12 February 2022, makes the spouse or partner ('cónyuge o conviviente') of a temporary resident eligible for a dependant permit and provides: 'Los dependientes estarán habilitados para realizar actividades remuneradas.' The restrictions the regulation may set apply only to the children (numeral 2). For spouses of Chileans and permanent residents, Decreto 177 art. 15 states that holders of the family-reunification permit 'podrán desempeñar actividades lícitas remuneradas'. Both provisions point to 'Yes, unrestricted right to work'. This is a disagreement with the first coder, not a change in the law.
answers.notes: Following the instructions, the starting answer is kept for both dates because no dated event explains a difference.

answers.implementation_then_now: No shift is documented. ENCLA 2023 (reported 2025) shows that migrants are concentrated in lower-paid jobs. Contract stability also varies by nationality: 85.6% of Venezuelan employees have open-ended contracts, while Haitians mostly have per-job contracts. The 2025 TIP Report records labour-trafficking cases among foreign victims, and the 2024 US human-rights report finds labour-law enforcement generally effective but inspectorate staffing insufficient. Before 2023, the 2022 TIP Report shows a similar picture. The starting rating is carried forward for both dates.

Informality, precarious contracts and labour exploitation of migrants are documented, and the inspectorate is reported understaffed. 'Usually' would be the MRD's usual rating where the law is honoured with known gaps. The legal answer itself holds: art. 14 of Ley 21.325 provides 'los mismos derechos en materia laboral que los chilenos'.

Neither source shows a clear shift in the window, so 'Usually' is kept for both dates.
